More than a decade ago, a question from UC Davis veterinary students sparked an idea: Could innovative cancer immunotherapy being used in people be adapted to help dogs? That question set in motion years of research by Dr. Stephen McSorley and collaborators, ultimately leading to a clinical trial testing a novel canine PDL1 antibody for dogs with advanced metastatic cancer. One of those patients was Snoopy, a 12-year-old beagle with large cancerous nodules in his lungs. After treatment, follow-up X-rays and CT scans showed the tumors had disappeared. For Snoopy's family, the results were life-changing. For the researchers, his response represents an important step in translating decades of basic science into potential new treatments for veterinary patients. ##### The Story Behind the Cat Cancer Study

Dr. Jennifer Grandis

8mo

When I spoke recently at The Ohio State University, I shared the story behind a study that started with a simple conversation with my sister, a veterinarian in Pittsburgh. She told me her clinic sees two cats a month with oral cancer, and every one of them dies. That reality inspired our University of California, San Francisco team to partner with veterinary oncologists at University of California, Davis and launch a clinical trial in pet cats with oral cancer. The results, featured in the San Francisco Chronicle and The Scientist, showed that a new drug could shrink tumors in cats AND potentially guide new treatments for people facing similar cancers. It’s a powerful reminder that collaboration across species and disciplines can lead to unexpected breakthroughs. # NC State Students Learn Oncology with Cancer Patients

Animal Cancer Center at NC State University

429 followers

3w

What if veterinary students could learn oncology…right alongside cancer patients? At NC State College of Veterinary Medicine, our preclinical veterinary students have a unique opportunity to join the oncology team for cageside rounds. During these sessions, students interact directly with patients in the hospital and join discussions about diagnoses, treatment options, prognosis, and the clinical decision-making that guides their care. It’s an opportunity to connect classroom learning with real patients and real-world cancer care, before students even begin their clinical rotations. Just as importantly, they get an early glimpse into the human side of veterinary oncology: communicating complex information, navigating treatment decisions, and caring for both patients and their families. We’re proud to give our students a chance to learn, ask questions, and see oncology in action! #NCState #AnimalCanerCenter #VeterinaryMedicine

# Kopra Bio raises $9.1M for cancer cell reprogramming therapy

Y Combinator

1,846,294 followers

4mo

Kopra Bio has raised $9.1M in seed funding to reprogram cancer cells to make cancer cures. Solid tumors represent approximately 90% of cancers worldwide, and the majority of cases can hide from the immune system, making them resistant to immunotherapies, the most successful cancer drugs of all time. Kopra's approach is different: a genetically engineered virus that turns the tumor into a biofactory for therapeutic proteins, exposing it to the immune system and recruiting T and NK cells to finish the job. They just published their work in Nature Communications, demonstrating long-term survival and durable tumor-specific immunity in aggressive brain cancer models. With this funding, Kopra is rapidly advancing its lead program into a clinical trial for glioblastoma in China, a faster path to first-in-human data for cell and gene therapies. Congrats on the round, Andrew Bartynski, Alexander Haddad, and team on the round! https://lnkd.in/gbCSawny

Y Combinator 📌 Some of the most profound innovations emerge when we stop asking how to fight disease harder and start asking how to fight it smarter. The ability to reprogram biological systems to work with the immune system rather than around it could reshape the future of cancer treatment. Congratulations to the Kopra Bio team on this milestone. Scientific breakthroughs begin in laboratories, but their true impact is measured in lives changed.

# Convocan a perros y gatos con diagnóstico queratosis actínica y carcinoma de células escamosas cutáneo

## La convocatoria de los investigadores de la Facultad de Ciencias Veterinarias de la Universidad Nacional de La Plata está destinada a pacientes caninos y felinos para participar de un ensayo clínico cuyos objetivos son evaluar aspectos diagnósticos, pronósticos y nuevas alternativas de tratamiento en estas enfermedades.

Foto: FCV-UNLP

Un equipo de investigadores de la Facultad de Ciencias Veterinarias de la Universidad Nacional de La Plata (FCV-UNLP) convoca a pacientes caninos y felinos con lesiones cutáneas pre-malignas -queratosis actínica y/o carcinoma de células escamosas in situ- para participar de un ensayo clínico cuyos objetivos son evaluar aspectos diagnósticos, pronósticos y nuevas alternativas de tratamiento en estas enfermedades.

Esta es una excelente oportunidad para que los tutores de perros y gatos con lesiones cutáneas pre-malignas puedan acceder al diagnóstico y tratamiento de estas lesiones en forma gratuita.

El desarrollo de estas lesiones pre-malignas se relaciona con la exposición crónica al sol en áreas de la piel con poco pelo y poco pigmento, y su presencia se asocia con un mayor riesgo de desarrollo de un tipo de cáncer de piel denominado carcinoma de células escamosas cutáneo.

Para poder participar, los tutores de los animales deberán completar un formulario al que se accede desde aquí y en caso de cumplir con los requerimientos serán contactados para coordinar un turno en el Hospital Escuela.

Este estudio se encuentra en el marco del Proyecto de Investigación “Potencial terapéutico de la vía de señalización mTOR en carcinomas de células escamosas cutáneos en caninos y felinos” dirigido por la Doctora Liyare Sanz Ressel, investigadora del Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas (CONICET) en la FCV-UNLP.

# Current Oncology Clinical Trials

Although we are making considerable progress in the fight against cancer, we still have a long way to go. Often, the best new information about cancer comes from animals participating in a clinical trial.

If you do not live in our region of the country, you could check with the Veterinary Cancer Society  to learn about clinical trials in your area.

## Emerging Canine Cancer Studies

We are currently recruiting for Emerging Canine Cancer Studies

  * High Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU) for Lymphoma in Dogs
  * High Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU) for Osteosarcoma in Dogs
  * Immunotherapy Trial of New Cancer Vaccine

Learn more about our Emerging Canine Cancer Studies

## Canine Urinary Bladder Cancer

For dogs with urinary bladder cancer (TCC) affecting the bladder and/or urethra. The study is aimed at learning how the dog’s immune system can be stimulated to attack the cancer.

Learn more about our Canine Urinary Bladder Cancer Trial

## Canine Osteosarcoma

The WCORC and Purdue Institute for Cancer Research have recently launched a research program in canine osteosarcoma to identify new, effective therapies in dogs that will improve cure rates for both dogs and humans with this cancer.

Our current focus is on collecting tumor tissues from dogs undergoing amputation to analyze them for susceptibility to novel drugs. A financial incentive of $500 per dog is available to help offset the cost of amputation to the owners of dogs contributing to this research.

We are excited to announce a new clinical trial for osteosarcoma that studies the clinical, molecular, and immune characterization of this tumor type. Eligible dogs must have a confirmed diagnosis, no evidence of metastasis, or spread, to other parts of the body, and received no prior treatment.

Learn more about our Clinical, Molecular, and Immune Characterization of Naturally-Occurring Osteosarcoma Clinical Trial

## Tumor Ablation Studies

H-FIRE Liver Cancer Study is evaluating the safety and immune effects of High-Frequency Irreversible Electroporation (H-FIRE) for dogs diagnosed with liver cancer.

The goals of this study are to evaluate the safety and feasibility of H-FIRE in dogs with liver cancer, measure local and systemic immune responses after H-FIRE treatment, analyze tumor biopsies, blood immune cells, and cytokines before and after treatment, and determine whether a single H-FIRE treatment can stimulate a meaningful anti-tumor immune response.

Learn more about our H-FIRE Liver Cancer Study

## Emerging Immunotherapy Study

Purdue is evaluating new immunotherapy approaches designed to help a dog's own immune system better recognize and fight cancer.  Currently, studies include evaluating MO29, a new drug that blocks SHP-1, a protein that can limit the immune system's response to cancer.

Learn more about SHP-1 inhibitor study

# Clinical Trials for Dogs with Cancer

Links last verified: August 20, 2026

## Explore Current Research Trials in Canine Oncology

When a beloved dog is diagnosed with cancer, many families ask whether a clinical trial may provide an additional option. Canine oncology studies are conducted throughout the United States and around the world, but identifying an appropriate trial, and participating in one, can sometimes be challenging.

Each clinical trial has specific eligibility requirements.

These may include: 

  * A dog’s breed
  * Age
  * Weight
  * Overall health
  * Life expectancy
  * Cancer type
  * Cancer stage
  * Previous care
  * ...and other medical factors

Meeting a study’s general description does not guarantee acceptance. Pet parents should speak directly with the research team and their veterinary care provider to determine whether a trial may be appropriate for their dog.

It is also important to understand that clinical trials are not always free.

Research funding may cover only certain tests, medications, procedures, or appointments. Families may still be responsible for additional veterinary expenses, travel, lodging, and repeated visits over several weeks or months, especially when a study is located far from home.

The following links are intended to help pet parents and veterinary professionals find information about current canine oncology trials being conducted throughout the United States and, in some cases, internationally.

We encourage families to carefully review each study’s eligibility requirements, location, potential costs, time commitment, and possible benefits and risks with their veterinary team.

Search the AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry

## Start Here: Nationwide Search Tools

If you are not sure where to begin, start with the AVMA registry. It lets you search by cancer type and by location, which is faster than checking individual centers one at a time.

#### AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry

The AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry, formerly known as the AVMA Animal Health Studies Database, helps dog parents and veterinary professionals find veterinary clinical studies taking place throughout the United States and Canada.
